quiz.title: Module 2 — Developing a Strong Speaking Voice
quiz.description: Monday's quiz covers the elements of vocal communication — rate of speech, volume, pitch, tonality and pausing — plus varying pace, pausing to let listeners process, handling nerves, pronunciation with a second language, neutral ears, and learning from effective speakers.

questions.prompt: Which five elements form the foundation of effective vocal communication?
options: Grammar, spelling, vocabulary, gestures, and posture
Rate of speech, volume, pitch, tonality, and pausing
Confidence, appearance, facial expressions, and eye contact
Listening, writing, reading, and speaking
questions.explanation: These five are the working controls of delivery. The others matter to communication, but they are not the vocal elements you adjust while speaking.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to vary your rate of speech when speaking to an audience?
options: It makes the speech longer.
It prevents the audience from asking questions.
It keeps listeners engaged and helps emphasize important points.
It makes every sentence sound the same.
questions.explanation: A steady pace flattens a speech. Slowing down or speeding up is how a speaker signals that something matters and pulls attention back.

questions.prompt: When preparing to answer the question "Tell me about yourself," what is the most effective approach?
options: Share every personal detail about your life.
Give a relevant story that demonstrates your experience, values, and connection to the role.
Memorize a long speech without considering your audience.
Avoid mentioning your experience or achievements.
questions.explanation: The question is an invitation to frame yourself in relation to what you are being considered for. A relevant story does that; a recital of biography does not.

questions.prompt: Which strategy can help reduce nervousness before public speaking?
options: Avoid preparing until the last minute.
Speak as quickly as possible to finish early.
Focus only on what could go wrong.
Practice breathing techniques, engage in light physical activity, and focus on the audience.
questions.explanation: Breathing and light movement settle the body, and turning attention outward to the audience takes it off the speaker's own anxiety.

questions.prompt: What is one important purpose of pausing during a speech?
options: To give listeners time to process information and give the speaker time to think.
To make the audience lose interest.
To avoid emphasizing important points.
To replace the need for preparation.
questions.explanation: A pause serves both sides at once: it lets the point land and gives the speaker a moment to collect the next thought.

questions.prompt: What is a useful way to improve pronunciation when speaking a second language?
options: Avoid speaking the language until you are fluent.
Speak as quickly as possible.
Record yourself speaking and seek feedback from qualified professionals, such as a speech-language pathologist or language teacher.
Focus only on learning new vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Recording reveals what you cannot hear while speaking, and informed feedback turns that into something you can correct. Waiting for fluency delays the practice that produces it.

questions.prompt: In communication, what does the idea of having "neutral ears" mean?
options: Speaking without changing your tone.
Practicing in complete silence.
Listening only to people who agree with you.
Practicing with people who have no fixed expectations about your usual communication style.
questions.explanation: People who know you hear what they expect from you. A listener with no assumptions gives you accurate feedback on what you actually said.

questions.prompt: Why can observing and imitating effective communicators help you improve your speaking skills?
options: It allows you to avoid developing your own communication style.
It helps you learn effective techniques that you can adapt to develop your own style.
It guarantees that every audience will respond positively.
It removes the need to practice speaking.
questions.explanation: Imitation is a starting point for finding your own approach, not a substitute for it. You borrow techniques and adapt them until they fit you.
